components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
贝 (shell, an ancient form of money) — 赛 originally related to offering valuables, later coming to mean 'to compete.'
宀 (mián) gives a sound distantly related to sài, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 这场大赛吸引了很多观众。
example.pinyin: Zhè chǎng dàsài xīyǐn le hěn duō guānzhòng.
example.english: This grand competition attracted a lot of spectators.
example.fact: 大赛 pairs 大 (“big”) directly with 赛 (“to compete, contest”) to mean a large-scale, high-stakes competition — distinguishing it from a plain 比赛 (“match, competition”), 大赛 signals something like a national or international tournament, on the scale of a World Cup or Olympics.

components.note: 开 (open, here representing a frame or opening) — 形 pictures light passing through a gap.
彡 (streaks or rays of light) — light and pattern coming through an opening gave 形 its meaning 'shape' or 'form.'
豕 (pig/boar) — appears as part of 象's original full-body pictograph of an elephant, reusing a four-legged-animal shape; 象 itself depicts an elephant's trunk and ears above the body.

example.hanzi: 这家公司很重视自己的形象。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngsī hěn zhòngshì zìjǐ de xíngxiàng.
example.english: This company places great importance on its own image.
example.fact: 形 (built from 开 “a gap or opening” plus 彡 “streaks of light” — light and pattern passing through an opening) and 象 (originally a pictograph of an elephant's trunk and ears, later broadened to “likeness, appearance”) combine into something like “shape and likeness,” giving 形象 its modern sense of a public or mental “image.”

components.note: 牛 (ox/cattle) — cattle were among the earliest and most valuable kinds of property, connecting 物 to the general idea of 'object' or 'thing.'
勿 (wù) gives the sound — 物 is also pronounced wù, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 我们要学会全面地看待事物。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yào xuéhuì quánmiàn de kàndài shìwù.
example.english: We need to learn to look at things comprehensively.
example.fact: 事物 is more abstract than 东西 (“thing,” a concrete physical object) — 事物 covers both tangible objects and intangible matters or phenomena, which is why it shows up constantly in philosophy and formal writing where 东西 would sound too casual.

components.note: 衣 (clothing) — 袋 names something made of cloth or similar material, a bag.
代 (dài) is an exact match for the sound of 袋.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 她把苹果放进了袋子里。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ píngguǒ fàng jìn le dàizi lǐ.
example.english: She put the apples into the bag.
example.fact: 代 (dài, “generation, to substitute”) supplies 袋's sound almost perfectly, while 衣 (“clothing, cloth”) marks its semantic category — a small reminder that early bags in China were most often sewn from cloth rather than made of other materials.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) shows 疯 describes an afflicted state of mind.
风 (fēng) gives the exact sound of 疯.

example.hanzi: 他因为压力太大都快发疯了。
example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi yālì tài dà dōu kuài fāfēng le.
example.english: He's almost going crazy from all the pressure.
example.fact: 疯 is built from 疒 (“sickness,” the same radical behind 症状's 症, also in this batch) over the phonetic 风 (“wind”) — pairing wind with the sickness radical reflects an old folk belief that madness could be stirred up by a kind of invisible wind disturbing the body.

components.note: 夕 (evening, night) — divination was traditionally done in the evening.
卜 (to divine, reading cracks in bone or shell) — combined with 夕 (evening), an evening divination was for unusual or 'outside' matters, giving 外 its meaning of 'outside' or 'foreign.'

example.hanzi: 除了周末以外,我每天都要上班。
example.pinyin: Chúle zhōumò yǐwài, wǒ měitiān dōu yào shàngbān.
example.english: Apart from weekends, I have to go to work every day.
example.fact: 以外 usually appears attached after 除了 (“apart from”) in the fixed frame “除了...以外,” even though 除了 alone can already mean “apart from” — a doubling-up of the same logic that mirrors how 因为...所以... keeps both halves in everyday speech.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — rope is made by twisting thread or fiber together.
黾 (mǐn) gives a sound distantly related to shéng, having drifted apart over time.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 请帮我把绳子系紧。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bāng wǒ bǎ shéngzi jì jǐn.
example.english: Please help me tie the rope tight.
example.fact: 绳 pairs the thread radical 纟 with the phonetic 黾 (mǐn, literally “frog, toad”) — an old borrowing purely for sound, since frogs have no real connection to rope-making, and the link has faded further as shéng and mǐn have drifted apart over the centuries.

components.note: 圣 is the simplified form of 聖, which combined an ear (耳, listening) and a mouth (口, speaking) above a standing figure — the image of someone who listens and speaks with special insight, giving 圣 its meaning 'holy, sacred.'
纟 (silk/thread) — 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving.
工 (gōng) gives a related sound cue for 经 (jīng), reflecting an older, closer pronunciation link between the two.

example.hanzi: 他每天晚上都会读《圣经》。
example.pinyin: Tā měitiān wǎnshang dōu huì dú Shèngjīng.
example.english: He reads the Bible every night.
example.fact: 圣 (built from 耳 “ear” and 口 “mouth” above a standing figure — someone who listens and speaks with special insight) plus 经 (“classic text, scripture”) literally suggest “holy scripture” — the same word 圣经 names both the Confucian classics and, in a Christian or Jewish context, the Bible, with context alone usually making clear which is meant.

components.note: 丁 (a stylized handle/hook shape in the ancient form) — part of the character's original picture, now mostly opaque in the modern form
口 (kǒu, mouth) gives a sound related to 可's pronunciation kě, and may connect to 可's sense of approval spoken aloud
Originally a drawing of a bear, with 厶 as its head, ⺼ as its body, and 匕匕 as its claws; the picture was later borrowed to mean 'ability, to be able to.'
忄 (heart/mind) — 性 relates to inner nature or character.
生 (shēng) gives a hint of the sound — 性 is pronounced xìng, a related sound though the initial has shifted.

example.hanzi: 这件事成功的可能性很大。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì chénggōng de kěnéngxìng hěn dà.
example.english: The possibility of this succeeding is high.
example.fact: Tacking the suffix 性 (“-ness, -ity”) onto the existing word 可能 (“possible, maybe”) is a fully regular process for turning an adjective into an abstract noun — the same pattern turns 重要 (“important”) into 重要性 (“importance”) and 可靠 (“reliable”) into 可靠性 (“reliability”).

components.note: 另 (other, separate) — 别 relates to distinguishing one thing from another.
刂 (knife) — cutting things apart to sort them gave 别 its meaning 'to separate' or 'other,' and later, 'don't' as a command.
辶 (to walk/move) — 选 relates to the process of selecting, as if moving through options
先 (xiān) gives a sound close to 选's reading xuǎn

example.hanzi: 面对这种情况,我们别无选择。
example.pinyin: Miànduì zhè zhǒng qíngkuàng, wǒmen bié wú xuǎnzé.
example.english: Faced with this situation, we have no other choice.
example.fact: Unlike many four-character idioms that lean on a classical story or allusion, 别无选择 is built transparently from its own parts — 别 (“other”), 无 (“without”), 选择 (“choice”) — so its meaning can be worked out directly from the pieces, making it one of the more approachable chengyu for learners.

components.note: 皿 (a vessel) — a chalice or bowl
丿 — a single drop of blood inside the vessel
辶 (to walk) — 迹 names the trace left behind by walking.
亦 (yì) gives a sound distantly related to jī, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 警察在现场发现了血迹。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zài xiànchǎng fāxiàn le xuèjì.
example.english: The police discovered bloodstains at the scene.
example.fact: 迹 pairs the “walking” radical 辶 with the phonetic 亦 (yì) to literally mean “a trace left by walking” — 血迹 extends that same image to blood left behind as a mark or trail, the logic behind other 迹-words like 足迹 (“footprint”) and 痕迹 (“trace, mark”).

components.note: 羊 (sheep; here representing feathers or ornaments on a headdress) — an elaborate decoration worn on the head.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — a person wearing a decorated headdress was seen as beautiful, giving 美 its meaning 'beautiful.'
口 (mouth) — 味 relates to taste, sensed in the mouth.
未 (wèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 味.

example.hanzi: 这家餐厅的菜非常美味。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā cāntīng de cài fēicháng měiwèi.
example.english: The food at this restaurant is extremely delicious.
example.fact: 美 (built from 羊, here representing an ornate headdress, plus 大, a person with arms outstretched — someone wearing a fine headdress was seen as “beautiful”) pairs with 味 (“taste, flavor”) to form 美味, quite literally “beautiful taste” — a word that works as both an adjective (“delicious”) and a noun (“a delicacy”).

components.note: 口 (mouths) — 总 pictures many voices.
心 (heart, mind) — many mouths brought together under one mind gave 总 its meaning 'overall' or 'to gather together.'
阝 (a variant of 邑, meaning place/settlement) — 部 relates to a division, section, or department.
咅 supplies the sound for 部 (bù); it belongs to the same phonetic family as related characters like 倍 (bèi) and 培 (péi).

example.hanzi: 这家公司的总部设在上海。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngsī de zǒngbù shè zài Shànghǎi.
example.english: This company's headquarters is located in Shanghai.
example.fact: 总 (built from 口 “mouths” over 心 “heart, mind” — many voices gathered under one mind) contributes the sense of “overall, chief”; attached to 部 (“department, section”), 总部 names the one central department that oversees all the others — literally the “chief branch.”

meanings: woman of similar age to one's parents

components.note: 阝 (a mound/place) — reflects 阿's original meaning related to a hill or slope
可 (kě) gives a sound close to 阿's reading ā
女 (woman) — 姨 names a female relative.
夷 (yí) gives the sound — an exact match with 姨.

example.hanzi: 楼下的阿姨每天都会来打扫。
example.pinyin: Lóu xià de āyí měitiān dōu huì lái dǎsǎo.
example.english: The auntie downstairs comes to clean every day.
example.fact: Beyond its literal sense of “maternal aunt,” 阿姨 has become the standard polite way to address any adult woman of roughly one's parents' age or a woman doing domestic or childcare work — much as 叔叔 (“uncle”) extends the same courtesy to men, letting speakers avoid a stranger's real name or a more distancing title.

meanings: to bring out implicit or innate qualities

components.note: 军 (army) — an army being directed
扌 (hand) — the hand giving the command or wave

example.hanzi: 他在比赛中充分发挥了自己的水平。
example.pinyin: Tā zài bǐsài zhōng chōngfèn fāhuī le zìjǐ de shuǐpíng.
example.english: He fully displayed his ability in the competition.
example.fact: 挥 pictures a hand 扌 giving a commanding wave, built on the phonetic 军 (“army”); combined with 发 (“to emit, send out”), 发挥 suggests something like “sending out with a wave of the hand” — an image that maps neatly onto its modern sense of bringing out hidden potential or ability.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.
宓 depicts stillness and quiet beneath a roof.
山 (mountain) — a quiet, secluded mountain gave 密 its meaning 'dense, secret, close.'

example.hanzi: 这份文件属于国家机密。
example.pinyin: Zhè fèn wénjiàn shǔyú guójiā jīmì.
example.english: This document is classified as a state secret.
example.fact: 机 (originally a wooden mechanism or device, such as a loom — from 木 “wood” plus 几, a stool-like shape) and 密 (a quiet, secluded place under a roof) combine into something close to “a hidden mechanism,” fitting 机密's modern sense of classified, need-to-know information.

components.note: 丶 (a dot) — represents the burning flame atop a lamp.
王 here depicts the base and stand of an oil lamp, not its usual meaning 'king' — the one who tends the flame became linked to 'master, lord, main.'
A drawing of a ridged, pointed animal horn.

example.hanzi: 她是这部电影的女主角。
example.pinyin: Tā shì zhè bù diànyǐng de nǚ zhǔjué.
example.english: She is the female lead of this movie.
example.fact: 角 is a pictograph of a ridged animal horn, later extended metaphorically to mean a dramatic “role” or “character” — much as English “horn” has no connection to acting, Chinese theater borrowed an unrelated physical object to name a stage part, and 主角 simply marks that role as the “main” (主) one.

components.note: 宀 (a roof, house) — 安 pictures shelter.
女 (woman) — a woman safely inside a house gave 安 its meaning 'peace' or 'safety.'
女 (woman) shows 娜 is typically used in women's names.
那 (nà) gives the exact sound of 娜.

example.hanzi: 安娜是我最好的朋友。
example.pinyin: Ānnà shì wǒ zuì hǎo de péngyou.
example.english: Anna is my best friend.
example.fact: 安娜 is a pure phonetic transliteration of the foreign name “Anna” — 安 (“peace, safety”) and 娜 (a character reserved almost exclusively for women's names) were chosen for their sound alone, not their meaning, the same strategy behind most transliterated foreign names in Chinese.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 纪 relates to organizing threads in order, extended to mean 'record, era'
己 (jǐ) gives a sound close to 纪's reading jì
今 (now, the present) — represents what is currently on one's mind.
心 (heart/mind) — keeping the present moment in mind gave 念 its meaning 'to think of, to read aloud, to study.'

example.hanzi: 我们买了一份礼物来纪念这个特别的日子。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen mǎi le yí fèn lǐwù lái jìniàn zhège tèbié de rìzi.
example.english: We bought a gift to commemorate this special day.
example.fact: 纪 (thread radical 纟 plus the phonetic 己) originally referred to keeping silk threads in order, extending to “record, era,” while 念 (今 “the present” over 心 “heart, mind”) means “to keep in mind” — together 纪念 suggests literally “recording in mind,” the mental act of holding onto a memory.

components.note: 入 (enter, put away) — 全 pictures something being placed into safekeeping.
玉 (jade) — a valuable treasure kept whole and undamaged, giving 全 its meaning of 'complete' or 'entire.'
王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — 球 originally referred to a round piece of jade, extended to mean 'ball, sphere'
求 (qiú) gives the sound — 球 is also pronounced qiú, an exact match

example.hanzi: 这个品牌在全球都很有名。
example.pinyin: Zhège pǐnpái zài quánqiú dōu hěn yǒumíng.
example.english: This brand is famous all over the world.
example.fact: 球 (built from 王, a variant of 玉 “jade,” plus the phonetic 求) originally named a round piece of carved jade before broadening to any “ball, sphere” — so 全球, literally “the whole ball,” treats the Earth as just another sphere, the same everyday metaphor English makes when it calls the planet “the globe.”

components.note: 言 (speech) — 警 relates to speaking out a warning or alarm
敬 (jìng) gives a sound close to 警's reading jǐng, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
宀 (roof) — 察 relates to careful observation
祭 (jì) gives a loose sound connection to 察's reading chá
尺 (a ruler/measure) — represents rules or measures being set.
口 (mouth) — measures being discussed aloud in one place gave 局 its meaning 'bureau, office, situation.'

example.hanzi: 他被带到了警察局做记录。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi dài dào le jǐngchájú zuò jìlù.
example.english: He was taken to the police station to give a statement.
example.fact: 警察局 stacks three meaning-bearing pieces — 警 (“to warn, alert”), 察 (“to observe, inspect”), and 局 (“bureau, office”) — into one compound; the first two alone, 警察, already form the standalone word for “police,” so 局 is simply appended to name the institution or building where they're based.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 倒 relates to a person falling over
到 (dào) gives the sound — 倒 is also pronounced dào, an exact match
雨 (rain) — 霉 relates to dampness, the condition that lets mold grow.
每 (měi) gives a sound close to méi, sharing the same rhyme with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 今天真倒霉,手机丢了。
example.pinyin: Jīntiān zhēn dǎoméi, shǒujī diū le.
example.english: Today is really unlucky — I lost my phone.
example.fact: 霉 pairs the “rain” radical 雨 with the phonetic 每 (měi) — dampness being the condition mold needs to grow — so 倒霉 literally suggests something like “mold has fallen [on you],” a vivid image behind Mandarin's everyday word for bad luck.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — part of the body.
匈 here representing an enclosed cavity, together giving 胸 its meaning 'chest, breast.'
阝 (a variant of 邑, meaning place/settlement) — 部 relates to a division, section, or department.
咅 supplies the sound for 部 (bù); it belongs to the same phonetic family as related characters like 倍 (bèi) and 培 (péi).

example.hanzi: 医生检查了他的胸部。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng jiǎnchá le tā de xiōngbù.
example.english: The doctor examined his chest.
example.fact: 部 (built from 阝, a variant of 邑 “settlement,” plus the phonetic 咅) generally marks off a “section” of something larger — attached to a body-part character, it turns a plain noun into a more clinical, anatomical term for that region, the same pattern behind 头部 (“head area”) and 腰部 (“waist area”).

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 忠 describes a heart that stays true, loyalty.
中 (zhōng) is an exact match for the sound of 忠.
讠 (speech) — 诚 relates to speaking honestly and sincerely.
成 (chéng) gives the sound — an exact match with 诚's reading chéng.

example.hanzi: 这只狗对主人非常忠诚。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhī gǒu duì zhǔrén fēicháng zhōngchéng.
example.english: This dog is extremely loyal to its owner.
example.fact: 忠 (心 “heart” plus the phonetic 中, zhōng — an exact sound match) and 诚 (讠 “speech” plus the phonetic 成, chéng — also an exact match) both combine a semantic radical with a phonetic that doubles as a perfect rhyme, a case where the character's sound-and-meaning construction is unusually transparent even after thousands of years.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 胡 originally referred to the flesh under an animal's chin or throat
古 (gǔ) gives the sound — an exact match with 胡's reading hú
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 爷爷留着一把白胡子。
example.pinyin: Yéye liú zhe yì bǎ bái húzi.
example.english: Grandpa has a full white beard.
example.fact: 胡 (⺼ “flesh,” originally the flesh under an animal's chin or throat, plus the phonetic 古) extended from “the area under the chin” to name what grows there — the beard — while 子 acts as a light, meaning-thin noun suffix, the same way it attaches to 桌子 (“table”) and 房子 (“house”).

components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
哥 doubles the character 可 ('to approve, to sing'), originally suggesting a call-and-response song between two singers; the meaning later narrowed to 'elder brother.'

example.hanzi: 他在家里是大哥,要照顾弟弟妹妹。
example.pinyin: Tā zài jiā lǐ shì dàgē, yào zhàogù dìdi mèimei.
example.english: He is the eldest brother in the family and has to look after his younger siblings.
example.fact: Beyond its literal family sense, 大哥 has become a common way to address a respected older male friend, a workplace senior, or even the head of a criminal gang — family vocabulary put to work as a marker of respect or hierarchy, the same extension seen in words like 老板 (“boss”) or 头儿 (“chief”).

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'
女 (woman) — 妞 (a girl) refers to a female person.
丑 (chǒu) gives a sound only distantly related to niū today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 那个小妞跑得真快。
example.pinyin: Nàge xiǎoniū pǎo de zhēn kuài.
example.english: That little girl runs really fast.
example.fact: 妞 is used almost exclusively to name young girls, built from 女 (“woman”) plus the phonetic 丑 (chǒu) — a sound link that has faded further than most, since niū and chǒu barely rhyme after roughly three thousand years of pronunciation change. As a colloquial, Northern-Mandarin-flavored word, 小妞 can sound affectionate among friends or condescending coming from a stranger, depending entirely on tone of voice.

components.note: 木 is the semantic element, tying the character's meaning to wood, a tree.
敢 (gǎn) is read identically to this character, "gǎn" — a clean phonetic match.
木 (tree) — 橄榄 (olive) is the fruit of a tree, so 榄 carries the wood/plant radical.
览 (lǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 榄's reading.
王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — 球 originally referred to a round piece of jade, extended to mean 'ball, sphere'
求 (qiú) gives the sound — 球 is also pronounced qiú, an exact match

example.hanzi: 美国人特别喜欢看橄榄球比赛。
example.pinyin: Měiguórén tèbié xǐhuan kàn gǎnlǎnqiú bǐsài.
example.english: Americans especially love watching football games.
example.fact: 橄榄球 literally means “olive ball” — 橄榄 (“olive”) is borrowed purely for its oval shape to name the sport's distinctively non-round ball, the same way an English speaker might informally describe an American football as “egg-shaped.”

components.note: 冂 (an enclosure or doorway) — 内 pictures the space one enters.
人 (person) — a person entering an enclosure gave 内 its meaning 'inside' or 'within.'

example.hanzi: 药物进入体内后开始起作用。
example.pinyin: Yàowù jìnrù tǐnèi hòu kāishǐ qǐ zuòyòng.
example.english: Once the medicine enters the body, it starts to take effect.
example.fact: 内 pictures a person 人 stepping into an enclosure 冂 — literally “entering an enclosed space” — giving 体内 (“within the body”) a transparent, almost architectural logic, with the body treated as a container that has an inside and an outside, the same contrast captured by its opposite, 体外 (“outside the body,” used for lab work done outside a living organism).

components.note: 夕 (evening, night) — divination was traditionally done in the evening.
卜 (to divine, reading cracks in bone or shell) — combined with 夕 (evening), an evening divination was for unusual or 'outside' matters, giving 外 its meaning of 'outside' or 'foreign.'
日 (sun) — 星 relates to bright heavenly bodies like the sun and stars
生 (shēng) gives a sound close to 星's reading xīng
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 这部电影讲的是外星人入侵地球的故事。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng jiǎng de shì wàixīngrén rùqīn dìqiú de gùshi.
example.english: This movie is about aliens invading Earth.
example.fact: 外星人 breaks down with unusual transparency into “outside” (外) + “star” (星) + “person” (人) — literally “a person from an outside star” — built the same way as its shorter cousin 外国人 (“foreigner,” literally “a person from an outside country”).

meanings: when all is said and done

components.note: 十 here relates to completeness, since 十 (ten) is a round, whole number.
比 (bǐ) gives a sound distantly related to bì, having drifted apart over time.
音 (music/sound) — a musical piece being performed
儿 (a person) — the performer finishing the piece

example.hanzi: 毕竟他还是个孩子,不能要求太高。
example.pinyin: Bìjìng tā háishi ge háizi, bù néng yāoqiú tài gāo.
example.english: After all, he's still a child, so we can't expect too much.
example.fact: 毕竟 typically opens a clause that reminds the listener of an underlying, easily-overlooked reason — much like English “after all” — and it pairs naturally with a following clause that softens an earlier claim or draws a more forgiving conclusion.

components.note: 土 (here representing a person swinging their arms, not its usual meaning 'earth') — depicts someone in motion.
止 (a foot) — combined with the moving figure above, 走 shows a person walking or running.
广 (a building, shelter) — a corridor is part of a building.
郎 (láng) gives the sound — an exact match for 廊.

example.hanzi: 学生们在走廊里排队。
example.pinyin: Xuéshengmen zài zǒuláng lǐ páiduì.
example.english: The students are lining up in the corridor.
example.fact: 走 (a person swinging their arms while moving, from a stylized moving figure over 止 “a foot”) supplies the idea of passing through, while 廊 (广 “a building” plus the phonetic 郎, láng) names a covered walkway — together 走廊 literally suggests a “walking-building,” a structure built specifically for passing through.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 墙 names a structure traditionally built from packed earth or brick.
啬 (sè) gives a sound distantly related to qiáng, having drifted apart over time.
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 墙上挂着一幅画。
example.pinyin: Qiángshang guà zhe yì fú huà.
example.english: A painting is hanging on the wall.
example.fact: 墙上 follows one of Mandarin's most productive patterns for saying “on/at [a place]” — attaching the light, neutral-toned 上 directly after a location noun, no preposition needed, the same pattern behind 桌上 (“on the table”), 身上 (“on the body”), and 路上 (“on the road”).

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 症 names a symptom or disease.
正 (zhèng) is an exact match for the sound of 症.
犬 (dog) — an old, now-opaque link behind 状's meaning 'form, shape, condition'
丬 (qiáng) gives a loose sound connection to 状's reading zhuàng

example.hanzi: 医生问我有什么症状。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng wèn wǒ yǒu shénme zhèngzhuàng.
example.english: The doctor asked me what symptoms I had.
example.fact: 症 pairs the “sickness” radical 疒 (the same radical behind 发疯's 疯, also in this batch) with the phonetic 正 (zhèng, an exact sound match), while 状 contributes the sense of “condition, form” — together naming the visible “form a sickness takes,” which is exactly what a symptom is.

components.note: 衤 (clothing) — the cloth that is about to be cut
刀 (a knife) — cutting the cloth is the first step in making clothes

example.hanzi: 我当初就不该答应这件事。
example.pinyin: Wǒ dāngchū jiù bù gāi dāying zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: I shouldn't have agreed to this in the first place.
example.fact: 当初 almost always signals hindsight — it frames a past moment specifically so the speaker can comment on how things have (or haven't) turned out since, which is why it shows up constantly in regret-tinged sentences built on the pattern “当初就不该...” (“shouldn't have... back then”).

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 道 relates to a path or road one walks along.
首 (shǒu) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer resembles dào, a reminder that sound components can drift after thousands of years of pronunciation change.
心 (heart/mind) — 德 relates to inner moral character and virtue.

example.hanzi: 说谎是不道德的行为。
example.pinyin: Shuōhuǎng shì bù dàodé de xíngwéi.
example.english: Lying is an immoral act.
example.fact: 道德 joins two words that are each philosophically loaded on their own — 道 (“the Way,” a central concept in Daoist and Confucian thought referring to the natural or moral order of the universe) and 德 (“virtue,” inner moral character) — so unlike English “morality,” which traces back to Latin mores (“customs”), 道德 carries an explicit metaphysical undertone straight from classical Chinese philosophy.

components.note: 目 (eye) — 睡 relates to closing the eyes to sleep.
垂 (chuí) gives a sound partly close to shuì, sharing part of the rhyme.

example.hanzi: 他躺下没多久就睡着了。
example.pinyin: Tā tǎng xià méi duō jiǔ jiù shuìzháo le.
example.english: He fell asleep not long after lying down.
example.fact: 着 is one of Mandarin's most read-dependent characters: as zháo, attached after 睡, it marks a completed action (“succeeded in falling asleep”), while the very same character elsewhere serves as the toneless aspect particle zhe marking an ongoing action (as in 有着, also in this batch) — the correct reading depends entirely on grammatical role, with no visual cue in the character itself.

components.note: 宀 (a roof, house) — 安 pictures shelter.
女 (woman) — a woman safely inside a house gave 安 its meaning 'peace' or 'safety.'
心 (heart) shows 慰 relates to an emotional state.
尉 (wèi) gives the exact sound of 慰.

example.hanzi: 朋友难过时,我们应该安慰她。
example.pinyin: Péngyou nánguò shí, wǒmen yīnggāi ānwèi tā.
example.english: When a friend is sad, we should comfort her.
example.fact: 安 (a woman 女 sheltered safely under a roof 宀, giving the sense of “peace, safety”) pairs with 慰 (心 “heart” plus the phonetic 尉, wèi) to form 安慰 — literally something like “putting the heart at peace,” a compositional logic that maps almost directly onto its English translation “to comfort.”

components.note: 糸 (thread/silk) — 系 relates to connecting or tying things together, like threads linking into a system.
刂 (a knife, related to 刀) — cutting and arranging pieces in order ties to 列's meaning 'row, line, to arrange'

example.hanzi: 他提出了一系列新的想法。
example.pinyin: Tā tíchū le yí xìliè xīn de xiǎngfǎ.
example.english: He proposed a series of new ideas.
example.fact: 系列 is almost always preceded by 一 in the fixed phrase 一系列 (“a series of, a whole set of”) — 系 already carries a sense of “linking, connecting” (from 糸, thread or silk), so 系列 layers “linked” over “arranged in a row” (列) to picture items strung together in sequence.

components.note: 月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.

example.hanzi: 这座城市有着悠久的历史。
example.pinyin: Zhè zuò chéngshì yǒuzhe yōujiǔ de lìshǐ.
example.english: This city has a long and storied history.
example.fact: 有着 is functionally almost identical to plain 有 (“to have”), but the added particle 着 gives it a more literary, descriptive flavor suited to writing — it appears constantly in essays and formal descriptions (“有着...的历史/意义/特点”) but can sound stilted in casual speech, where bare 有 is the natural choice.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — muscle is a kind of body tissue.
几 (jǐ) gives the sound — a close match for jī, differing only in tone.
冂 traces the outer outline of a cut of meat.
仌 depicts the muscle fibers or ribs inside, together forming a picture of a piece of meat.

example.hanzi: 他经常锻炼,肌肉很发达。
example.pinyin: Tā jīngcháng duànliàn, jīròu hěn fādá.
example.english: He exercises regularly, so his muscles are well developed.
example.fact: 肌 (⺼ “flesh” plus the phonetic 几, jǐ) and 肉 (a pictograph of a cut of meat, its outline 冂 wrapping around lines 仌 that suggest muscle fiber or ribs) both independently mean roughly “flesh, meat” — 肌肉 doubles up two near-synonyms from the same semantic field into one specific, modern word for “muscle.”

components.note: 亻 (person) — 保 relates to a person looking after or protecting someone, originally a caretaker holding a child.
呆 (dāi) gives a hint of the sound — 保 is pronounced bǎo, a connection that has shifted over time.
千 (thousand) — 重 pictures a heavy burden carried a great distance.
里 (a unit of distance, like a mile) — carrying something a thousand 里 emphasizes how heavy and significant a burden it is, giving 重 its meaning 'heavy' or 'important.'

example.hanzi: 天气冷了,你要多保重身体。
example.pinyin: Tiānqì lěng le, nǐ yào duō bǎozhòng shēntǐ.
example.english: The weather's gotten cold — you should take good care of your health.
example.fact: 保重 is one of the most common ways to close a letter, phone call, or goodbye in Chinese, roughly matching English “take care” — 保 (a person 亻 looking after someone, historically a caretaker holding a child) plus 重 (“heavy, important”) suggests literally “guard what is important [your health].”

components.note: 禾 (grain, a rice/wheat plant) — 科 relates to sorting and measuring crops.
斗 (a measuring ladle) — measuring grain into ordered categories gave 科 its meaning 'a branch of study' or 'a department.'
冖 (a covering/roof) — represents the building or schoolhouse where learning happens.
子 (child) — 学 depicts children gathered to study.
⺍ is a small graphic element at the top of the character; its original pictorial meaning, if any, has been lost over time.
宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.

example.hanzi: 这位科学家发现了一种新元素。
example.pinyin: Zhè wèi kēxuéjiā fāxiàn le yì zhǒng xīn yuánsù.
example.english: This scientist discovered a new element.
example.fact: 家 as a suffix meaning “an expert or practitioner of X” turns 科学 (“science”) into 科学家 (“scientist”) the same way it turns 音乐 (“music”) into 音乐家 (“musician”) and 艺术 (“art”) into 艺术家 (“artist”) — one of Mandarin's most reliable, productive suffixes for naming a professional in a field.

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — the state of mind being described.
夬 (a decisive, resolute action) — a resolute state of mind, giving 快 its meaning 'fast, quick.'
女 (woman) with 覀 depicting hands on the waist — an old image of insisting or demanding something, connected to 要's meaning 'to want, to need.'

example.hanzi: 火车快要到站了。
example.pinyin: Huǒchē kuàiyào dào zhàn le.
example.english: The train is about to arrive at the station.
example.fact: 快要 almost always appears together with a sentence-final 了 to mark an imminent change of state, in the pattern “快要...了” (“about to...”) — the same “time adverb + 了” pairing that shows up with 已经 (“already”), making 了 one of the hardest-working single characters in Mandarin grammar.

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 震 originally described thunder shaking the sky along with a storm.
辰 (chén) gives a sound distantly related to zhèn, having drifted apart over time.
忄 (heart) — 惊 relates to an emotional reaction of shock or fright
京 (jīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 惊's reading jīng

example.hanzi: 这个消息让所有人都感到震惊。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiāoxi ràng suǒyǒu rén dōu gǎndào zhènjīng.
example.english: This news left everyone feeling shocked.
example.fact: 震 (雨 “rain” plus the phonetic 辰, chén) originally described thunder rumbling through a storm, while 惊 (忄 “heart” plus the phonetic 京, jīng — an exact sound match) names a startled emotional jolt — together 震惊 pairs a natural, physical shock with a psychological one.

components.note: 女 (woman) — an older semantic link to leisure and enjoyment.
吴 (wú) gives a sound close to yú, sharing the same final.
乐 is the simplified form of 樂, which depicted a wooden 木 instrument strung with strings 幺, played with a pick 白 — music came to represent joy, giving 乐 its meaning 'happy, music.'

example.hanzi: 周末我喜欢参加一些娱乐活动。
example.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒ xǐhuan cānjiā yìxiē yúlè huódòng.
example.english: On weekends I like to take part in some entertainment activities.
example.fact: 乐 is the simplified form of 樂, traditionally analyzed as a wooden instrument 木 strung with strings 幺 and played with a pick — music's association with joy gave 乐 its double life as both “happy” (lè) and “music” (yuè), two related but distinct readings of the same character depending on context.

components.note: 厂 (a cliff or overhang) — 反 pictures pushing against a steep surface.
又 (a hand) — a hand pushing back against a cliff gave 反 its meaning 'to turn over' or 'opposite.'
扌 (hand) — fighting back with bare hands
亢 — the throat, a vulnerable point defended while resisting

example.hanzi: 人民奋起反抗压迫。
example.pinyin: Rénmín fènqǐ fǎnkàng yāpò.
example.english: The people rose up to resist oppression.
example.fact: 反 (a hand 又 pushing back against a cliff 厂, giving the sense of “to turn over, oppose”) and 抗 (a hand 扌 defending the throat 亢, a vulnerable point) both independently picture physical resistance — 反抗 doubles up two body-based images of pushing back into one word for active resistance.

components.note: The repeated 口 (mouth) shapes are thought to represent cries of alarm or distress, tying into the character's meaning of 'shocking, ill-omened.'
林 here depicts eyes shut in sleep, not its usual meaning 'forest.'
夕 (evening, night) — sleeping at night is when dreams occur, giving 梦 its meaning 'dream.'

example.hanzi: 我昨晚做了一个噩梦。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zuówǎn zuò le yí gè èmèng.
example.english: I had a nightmare last night.
example.fact: 噩 pictures repeated 口 (“mouth”) shapes, thought to represent cries of alarm or distress — stacking that ominous character directly onto 梦 (“dream,” built from eyes shut in sleep over 夕 “night”) gives 噩梦 a vivid, almost onomatopoeic image: a dream filled with screaming.

components.note: 心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.
火 (fire) — linked to ritual fires once used to try to communicate with spirits
彐 (jì) gives a sound distantly related to 灵's reading líng, having drifted apart considerably over time

example.hanzi: 音乐可以治愈人的心灵。
example.pinyin: Yīnyuè kěyǐ zhìyù rén de xīnlíng.
example.english: Music can heal the human soul.
example.fact: 心 is a pictograph of the physical shape of a heart, extended early on to also mean “mind, feelings”; 心灵 pairs it with 灵 (whose semantic root 火 “fire” ties back to ritual fires once used to try to communicate with spirits) to form a word that leans toward the more poetic, spiritual register of “soul” or “inner self,” distinct from the more everyday, emotional 心情 (“mood, feelings”).

components.note: 寸 (a hand) reaching for 旦 (originally 貝, a shell used as currency) — a picture of grasping something valuable, hence 'to obtain, to get.'

example.hanzi: 这是他应得的奖励。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì tā yīngdé de jiǎnglì.
example.english: This is the reward he deserves.
example.fact: 应得 combines 应 (“should, ought to” — also seen in 应该) with 得 (“to obtain, to get” — a hand 寸 reaching for a valuable shell 貝) to mean literally “ought to obtain,” giving Mandarin a compact single word for “deserve” where English needs a separate verb.
